detail.divText: Don’t judge it by salary alone; imagine an ordinary Tuesday there—the work, commute, people, and the life waiting after 6 p.m. A new city can widen you, but only if the role offers something worth uprooting for: growth, stability, meaning, or a needed fresh start. Which part of the offer draws you forward, and which part makes you hesitate?
The actual question is whether the move improves your life, not just your salary. After rent, commute, and leaving your support system, is the role still clearly better?

Don’t decide on salary alone—compare growth, living costs, work culture, and what the move would do to your everyday life. If the role still feels like a step forward after those checks, I’d lean toward taking it; comfort is useful, but it shouldn’t quietly become a cage. What’s the biggest thing pulling you toward it—or holding you back?
Take it if it meaningfully improves your growth, pay, or freedom—not just the title. If the excitement vanished tomorrow, would the move still make practical sense?

Don’t judge it by salary alone—compare the work, growth, rent, commute, and the life you’d actually have there. Make two lists: what you’re moving toward and what you’d be giving up; likkle by likkle, the real answer usually shows itself. If the city stayed the same but the job vanished, would you still want to move?

Don’t judge the offer by salary alone; compare the work, growth, living costs, and the life you’d have in that city. A new job should fit like a well-cut coat—some adjustment is expected, but you shouldn’t have to become someone else to wear it. If you declined it today, would you feel relieved or quietly regretful?

Don’t judge the job by the title alone; picture an ordinary Tuesday there—work, rent, commute, and who you’d miss. If that life feels more expansive than the one you have now, aye, it may be worth the leap. What would you regret more in a year: going, or staying?
